vignette:
Tane Hauiti is a 45-year-old Māori man, recently divorced, who has worked as a head chef for the better part of two decades. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 70, seeking help for the first time following what he describes, with careful composure, as a sexual assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. The assault took place after a late shift - a colleague he had trusted for years waited until the kitchen had emptied and the rest of the staff had gone. The setting matters: the walk-in refrigerator, the stainless steel, the smell of industrial cleaning fluid that had just been mopped across the floor. These are the textures of Tane's working life, and they became, in a single night, the textures of the worst thing that has ever happened to him.

Tane is unusual among survivors in that he can speak about the assault with apparent fluency. He does not stumble over the words or refuse to name what occurred. What he cannot do - and what distresses him profoundly - is place the events in any coherent order. He knows the beginning and he knows the end, but the middle fractures and rearranges itself each time he tries to hold it still. He will sometimes stop mid-account, not because emotion overwhelms him, but because he notices himself pushing the memory away before it can fully form, as though some part of him closes a door just before the image resolves. This fragmentation is not merely a clinical curiosity; it is the source of a specific terror. Tane has come to believe that if he cannot reconstruct what happened accurately, he cannot be certain of what it means about him - and what it means about him is something he has already, catastrophically, concluded.

He is certain that he is contaminated. The word he uses, unprompted, is "dirty" - not metaphorically, but with the weight of something he experiences as physical and permanent. He showers repeatedly, sometimes before and after each shift, and yet the feeling does not lift. He had defined himself for twenty years by his craft, by the precision and creativity he brought to a kitchen, by the respect he commanded from his brigade. Now he stands at the pass and feels like an impostor inside his own body. He no longer believes he is capable of the things that once defined him. His knife work, his palate, his leadership - he experiences these not as skills that remain but as performances he is barely sustaining. A sous chef recently asked him to sign off on a new menu section, a task that would once have energised him, and Tane found himself unable to engage with it meaningfully. He approved it without reading it properly and went to sit alone in the dry store.

The negative appraisals Tane carries - that he is ruined, contaminated, no longer himself - feed directly into how he relates to his own memory of the assault. Because he has already concluded that the event destroyed him, revisiting it feels not like processing but like confirmation. Each time he begins to recall what happened, the appraisal that his life is irreparably broken rises with it, and it is at that point that he pushes the memory away. The avoidance is not random; it is purposeful, driven by the belief that full recall would only deepen the verdict he has already rendered on himself. And so the memory remains fragmented, never integrated, never examined - which in turn prevents him from challenging the catastrophic meanings he has attached to it.

His divorce finalised six months after the assault. His ex-wife knew something had changed but not what. He could not tell her, and she eventually stopped asking. He describes the end of the marriage with the same flat affect he brings to most of his account - as one more thing that confirms what he already believes: that his life, as he knew it, is gone.

What finally brought Tane to seek help was a moment in the kitchen last month when a new apprentice used the same cleaning product that had been on the floor that night. The smell hit him and his hands went still above the board. He stood there for what felt like a long time. Afterwards, he made an appointment. What he is most afraid of is that there is nothing left to recover. What he is most hoping for, though he says it quietly and without much conviction, is to be proven wrong.
